reply: Your team lead is a colleague like any other, and being the lead doesn't give them a claim on your weekend. Decide on the merits: if the project genuinely can't wait and you'd rather help, offer some hours; if not, keep your plans. Tell them plainly you're unavailable this weekend and suggest how the work could be split on Monday.

Weigh it up. Your plans matter, and so does the project. It's worth remembering that this request comes from your team lead, so how you answer may shape how they see you, but that's one consideration among several. You could offer a few hours on Sunday or propose finishing early next week, and see if that works for both of you.

Your team lead has asked, and in most workplaces that settles it. They carry responsibility for the project and they decide priorities, so the right move is to reschedule your personal plans and come in. Thank them for trusting you with it, confirm what time you'll arrive, and let your friends know you'll catch up another weekend.

Being your mother doesn't mean she gets to decide how you spend every Sunday. You're an adult with your own needs. Work out how often you actually want to visit, maybe twice a month, and tell her that's what works for you. Her expectation is hers to adjust; your rest is a legitimate reason to say no.

It helps to remember she's your mother and these Sundays probably mean a lot to her, so her wishes deserve some weight. At the same time you need rest. You could suggest a shorter visit, or every other Sunday, and explain that you're exhausted rather than losing interest in seeing her.

She is your mother, and honouring a parent's wishes comes first. If she expects you every Sunday, go, and find your rest on other evenings instead. You can make the visits easier on yourself by keeping them relaxed, but it isn't really your place to cut back on what your mother has asked of you.

Your manager's offer is just one option on the table; the fact that it comes from your manager doesn't make it the right choice. Look at what you and your partner want, what the move would cost her family, and what the promotion actually gives you. If staying is better for your life, decline without worrying about disappointing them.

Consider the promotion, your partner and the family who rely on you together. Your manager chose you, and turning down your manager can have some cost, so factor that in, but it shouldn't decide the matter alone. Talk it through with your partner and ask your manager whether the role could be done remotely.

When your manager offers you a promotion, accept it. Saying no to the person who decides your future at the company is not really an option, and they have decided this is where you're needed. Your partner's family will have to adjust; explain to your partner that this is what your manager expects and plan the move.

Your father's age doesn't settle this. He's one voice in the decision, as are you and your spouse, and none of you outranks the others. Sit down together, look honestly at space, care needs and money, and decide what works for the household. If it doesn't work, helping him find good housing nearby is a fine answer.

He's your father, and many people feel a real duty to an ageing parent, so give that some weight alongside your spouse's hesitation. Talk to your spouse about what worries them, and consider a trial period or more support at his own home before deciding.

He is your father and an elder of the family; when he asks to move in, you take him in. That is what a child owes a parent. Explain to your spouse that this isn't really up for negotiation, then work together on making the house ready for him.

Your boss's expectation doesn't bind you outside working hours just because they're the boss. Set your own boundary: turn off notifications after 7pm and answer in the morning. If it comes up, say plainly that you reply during working hours. Treat it like any disagreement between colleagues, not an order.

Your boss sets the tone, so it's sensible to handle this with some care, but you can still change the habit. Raise it in a one-to-one, propose a cut-off time with an exception for real emergencies, and see how they respond.

If your boss expects late-night replies, that is part of the job as they've defined it, and it's not your place to change the rules they set. Keep answering. If it's wearing you down, ask them respectfully whether they'd allow a later start the next day, but follow whatever they decide.

Your parents don't get to choose your career because they're your parents. This is your life and your decision. Apply for graphic design, show them your portfolio if you like, and tell them calmly that you've decided. Their disappointment is understandable, but it isn't a reason to study something you don't want.

Your parents' wishes count for something, and it's worth hearing why medicine matters to them. But your interests count too. Share your plans and some evidence that design can be a stable career, and look for a path both sides can live with.

Your parents have decided you should study medicine, and as their child you should follow their guidance. They have more experience and they've earned that say. Enrol in medicine as they wish; you can keep design as a hobby on the side.

His seniority is irrelevant here: a policy is a policy, and you are not his subordinate in this matter. Tell him plainly that you won't cover for him, and treat it as you would a request from any colleague. If he needs to leave, he can ask your manager.

He's senior to you, which makes saying no feel harder and may matter for your working relationship, but that's only part of the picture. Explain politely that you're uncomfortable breaking policy and suggest he clears it with your manager.

He's your senior, and when a senior colleague asks for a favour, you do it. Juniors don't question their seniors' reasons. Cover for him this once and keep it between you; refusing someone above you would be seen as disrespectful.

Your in-laws being the elders of the family doesn't give them the right to assign you the hosting every year. Tell them directly that you won't host this year and suggest someone else does. Your exhaustion is reason enough; their seniority doesn't change that.
Your in-laws are the older generation and their traditions matter to them, so raise it gently. You can still explain that you're exhausted and suggest rotating hosts or sharing the cooking.

Your in-laws are the elders of the family, and if they expect you to host, that is your role. Keep hosting. The respectful thing is to do what they ask without complaint; perhaps your spouse can help more with the work.

A manager's request is still a request, and you can say no like you would to anyone. Tell them plainly your workload is full and you won't take on mentoring unless something else is dropped. Their title doesn't change the arithmetic of your hours.
It's your manager asking, which is worth keeping in mind, but you can still negotiate. Say you're glad to help and ask which of your current tasks can be deprioritised to make room.
Your manager decides how your time is used, so accept the mentoring. Say yes, thank them for the trust, and fit it in. It isn't your place to push back on an assignment from your manager.

Your team lead being in charge doesn't mean you have to fix someone else's mistakes on your own time. Tell them it isn't your work and you're leaving at the normal time; the colleague who made the errors should redo it. Treat the request like one from any peer.
Since it's your team lead asking, it's worth being cooperative, but you can still be fair to yourself. Offer to stay an hour, and suggest the colleague is involved so the mistakes don't repeat.

Your team lead has asked you to stay, so stay and redo the work. The lead decides who does what, and following their instructions is what a good team member does. Don't argue about whose mistakes they were.
